title: Migration Conflicts and Troubleshooting
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of migration conflicts and troubleshooting and at least two listed subtopics.
Interpret the migration conflicts and troubleshooting example and predict its expected result.
Choose a verification step and identify one version, security, data, or troubleshooting consideration.

content.intro: Learn migration conflicts and troubleshooting through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Migration Conflicts and Troubleshooting matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines migration conflicts and troubleshooting as part of database configuration, migrations, and transactions. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Conflicting migration branches; Merge migrations; Missing migration dependencies; Database schema drift; Diagnosing failed migrations. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Conflicting migration branches
items.text: Conflicting migration branches affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: Merge migrations
items.text: A migration is a versioned, ordered schema/data operation. `makemigrations` creates files; `migrate` applies them. Review generated operations and test the forward path and recovery plan using representative data.

items.title: Missing migration dependencies
items.text: Missing migration dependencies affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: Database schema drift

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Migration Conflicts and Troubleshooting
content_blocks.code:
python manage.py showmigrations
python manage.py makemigrations --check
python manage.py migrate --plan
content_blocks.expected_output: These commands inspect migration state, check for model changes without migration files, and show a plan to apply migrations.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open a local project using the documented Django 6.1-compatible Python environment. If this snippet depends on model names, URL configuration, settings, or an optional package, add those prerequisites before running it. Otherwise inspect it as a static example. CodeLeaf browser preview does not execute Django/Python server code.
content_blocks.troubleshooting: Do not delete or rewrite migration history as a quick fix. Review dependency graphs, backup and test the proposed migration on a safe database.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First identify the input and the responsible Django component. Next trace how the example moves through “Migration Conflicts and Troubleshooting” and the related concept “Conflicting migration branches”. Predict the result before running or inspecting it. Finally compare the observed behavior with the expected result and the cited official documentation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to Conflicting migration branches. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to describe migration conflicts and troubleshooting, explain the listed topics, inspect the example, and choose an appropriate verification step. Keep the scope and version caveat visible when sharing your solution.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a framework fragment without its imports, configuration, model, or URL context.
common_mistakes.why: The snippet may be incomplete when separated from a Django project.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the stated prerequisites and run the relevant management check or focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting input or relying only on a happy-path example.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid values, unauthorized requests, or concurrent activity can violate assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and add a negative or boundary test.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating the development sample as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Production hosting, secrets, storage, monitoring and resource limits differ from local use.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the current deployment/security references and document untested areas.
